articles.title: LG buys Homey in a very Samsung SmartThings move
articles.summary: LG has acquired an 80 percent stake in Athom, best known for its Homey smart home platform, in a deal that could help LG compete with Samsung’s SmartThings.
articles.body: LG has acquired an 80 percent stake in Athom, a Dutch company best known for its Homey smart home platform. The deal, which LG says will see it acquire the remaining 20 percent of Athom within the next three years, has been forged to expand LG’s smart home ecosystem and should position it to better compete against Samsung’s rivaling SmartThings platform. LG plans to integrate Athom’s existing Homey connectivity — which supports smart devices from Sonos, Ikea, Aqara, Philips Hue, and more — across its appliances through its ThinQ smart home platform. According to Homey, its users will soon be able to control ThinQ-enabled LG appliances via the platform. Homey has developed a significant user base since it was founded in 2014, with its flagship Homey Pro smart home hub capable of connecting to over 50,000 devices across Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Z-Wave, Matter, and Thread. The deal will enable LG to incorporate third-party devices and services into its ThinQ ecosystem for the first time. LG executive vice president Jung Ki-hyun refers to the Athom acquisition as “a cornerstone for our AI home business.” LG announced plans during CES in January to bring so-called “Affectionate Intelligence” to its ThinQ smart home platform — which Homey’s connection to appliances, sensors, and lighting may now play a part in. LG says that Athom will continue to operate as an independent company following the acquisition, retaining its current branding and operations. It’s a similar move to Samsung acquiring SmartThings for $200 million in 2014, which has since seen Samsung building multi-connectivity SmartThings support into soundbars, TVs, smart fridges, monitors, and more. “Homey will continue as it is, with Athom remaining committed to developing Homey Cloud and Homey Pro, and keep working on an ever-expanding lineup of new products,” said Homey in its acquisition statement. “Both the founders, Emile Nijssen & Stefan Witkamp, will stay on as executives of Athom, and continue to execute their vision and create a better smart home for everyone.” The value of the deal has not been officially disclosed, though The Korea Economic Daily reports that it’s estimated to be around 85 billion won ($61 million). LG also hasn’t clarified how Homey’s connectivity and integrations will be embedded into its products but notes that the deal will allow it to “gain deeper insights into customers’ lifestyle and usage patterns” — which may not mesh well with Homey’s “privacy first” ethos.

articles.title: Tim Cook was an innovator — just not the Jobs kind
articles.summary: Tim Cook didn’t have a mega-hit product during his tenure, but his time as Apple’s CEO remade the company into what it is today.
articles.body: Under Steve Jobs, Apple released the groundbreaking products that defined the company. But the company wouldn’t be what it is today without Tim Cook’s reign of ruthless efficiency. Jobs’ legacy has long been written at this point. He was stubborn, unpleasant, and a generational visionary. He pushed the limits of industrial design and brought technologies together in ways that others laughed off at the time. It’s an iconic tenure that’s basically unequaled anywhere else in tech. But the radical thinker passed the torch to a very different kind of CEO in Tim Cook in August of 2011. Tim Cook is an inventor of a different kind. The Apple Watch and AirPods both arrived in the Cook years, and under his direction the company made a bold and lucrative bet on bringing chip design in-house. Nothing to sneeze at. But I wouldn’t call any of those generational innovations on par with the iMac or the iPhone. Instead, Cook optimized Apple’s product lines and supply chains to turn the company into a revenue-generating machine. As my colleague Sean Hollister noted around the 10th anniversary of Cook’s appointment as CEO, on his watch, Apple’s value eclipsed a couple of Saudi state-owned oil companies. Tim Cook joined Apple in 1998 and quickly earned a reputation as a quiet, calculating supply chain wizard. He recognized a huge opportunity with Foxconn and expanded its relationship with the company, which was then only a minor supplier. He brought on like-minded former IBM colleagues, including future COO Jeff Williams and the famously ruthless negotiator Tony Blevins. They made huge investments in Foxconn that paid off for both companies. Apple managed unheard-of profit margins on the iPhone, and Foxconn became a trillion-dollar industry leader. Cook may not have been a Jobs-level product innovator, but he did figure out how to sell a hell of a lot of iPhones. Under Cook, Apple began targeting different market segments with model variants, experimenting with Plus, Mini, and R versions on its way to the five current models it sells today: the 17, 17E, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, and Air. The company set sales record after record. When growth stalled as people held onto their phones longer, another cash cow overtook hardware: services. Cook knew how to squeeze a supply chain, and that includes software. The company maintained an iron grip over the App Store on his watch, and levied an infamous 30 percent fee on transactions that took place there. App Store fees, along with revenue from its growing portfolio of subscription businesses like Apple Music and Apple TV, make up a category the company refers to as services. The sales that Apple attributes to services rank second only to the iPhone itself — bigger than the Mac, iPad, and wearables combined. In the fourth quarter of 2025, Apple attributed $30 billion worth of sales to the category. Tim Cook saw Apple through a decade of unprecedented growth, but the vibes started shifting in recent years. The company won a lawsuit brought by Epic Games centered on its App Store practices, but a federal judge ordered the company to relax its tight grip on App Store payments, a huge source of that services revenue. Four years later, the judge took Cook to task when she found the company’s weak attempts at reforms to be insufficient, saying that the CEO “chose poorly” at every turn. Malicious compliance was business as usual in the Cook era, but the second Donald Trump term has turned out to be the real watershed for the departing CEO’s legacy. He has taken every opportunity to appease the president, from presenting him with a gold-and-glass statue to attending a VIP screening of Melania, the $75 million not-a-bribe documentary distributed by Amazon. Following public backlash around ICE activity in Minnesota, Cook offered only a mealy-mouthed statement about the need for “deescalation.” When the Grok app was clearly being used to create nonconsensual sexual deepfakes of women, Apple quietly asked X’s developers to rein it in — but never actually penalized Elon Musk’s company. The values of inclusion and empowerment that Cook’s Apple publicly espoused proved to be a weaker force than shareholder value. [Image: Tim Cook takes the stage at WWDC in 2024. Cook’s departure has been long rumored, but comes at a particularly precarious time for the company. No amount of kissing the ring can buy President Trump’s good favor forever, even though Cook is sticking around the company to keep trying. Elsewhere, Apple continues to fight antitrust battles. The memory crisis has put pressure on the entire supply chain, threatening even Apple’s famously generous margins. But those who found the Cook era of predictable efficiency to be a bit boring can take heart: John Ternus is a hardware guy. The press release announcing Cook’s departure names the many product lines that Ternus oversaw as SVP of hardware engineering. But the first specific product highlighted in the memo isn’t the iPhone 17; it’s the MacBook Neo. Apple calls it “an all-new laptop that makes the Mac experience even more accessible to more people around the world,” and it’s not wrong. The Neo is surprisingly powerful for its low $599 price, and it’s a kind of culmination of the strengths Apple fostered in the Cook era. Cook oversaw the move to Apple designing its own silicon, which is how a previous-gen iPhone chip can be repurposed successfully in a brand-new laptop. Ruthless efficiency and supply chain mastery are their own kind of innovation. Tim Cook turned the company into a well-oiled machine; now we’ll find out what a hardware guy can do with it.

articles.title: Tim Cook’s departure is the start of a new era at Apple
articles.summary: When Tim Cook steps down as CEO of Apple in September, he’ll leave behind a team of executives who are even further removed from the Steve Jobs era.
articles.body: Apple is about to become a very different company. This September, Apple CEO Tim Cook is stepping down and will be replaced by John Ternus, the current head of hardware. But the shift is bigger than just a CEO transition — it’s the most significant move yet into a world where Apple’s executive team isn’t handpicked by Steve Jobs. With the departure of Cook, who became CEO in 2011, the list of leaders who were in Jobs’ inner circle is dwindling. There’s still Apple’s senior vice president of services, Eddy Cue, who joined in 1989, and has said that Jobs was like a “family member” to him. There’s also longtime marketing exec Phil Schiller, who worked with Jobs to launch key products, including the Mac, iPod, iPhone, and iPad, and often appeared with Jobs during keynotes. Schiller stepped into a smaller role in 2020, though he still oversees one major business, the App Store. [Image: Other top holdovers include Greg Joswiak and Craig Federighi. Joswiak started at Apple in 1986 and worked under Jobs for years, playing a role in launching the original iPod and iPhone. He later took Schiller’s spot as the head of marketing in 2020. Federighi, Apple’s software head, also had close ties to Jobs. He worked at Jobs’ technology company NeXT before it was acquired by Apple in 1996. Though Federighi left shortly after the acquisition, he rejoined Apple in 2009. But many key Jobs-era figures at Apple are gone. iOS leader Scott Forstall, who was once seen as a potential successor to Jobs, was pushed out a year into Cook’s tenure over the botched launch of Apple Maps. [Image: Bob Mansfield, a key part of Jobs’ executive team, finally stepped away after years of Cook pulling him back. He joined Apple through an acquisition in 1999 and later headed up the Mac’s transition to Intel processors. Mansfield nearly retired in 2012 but decided to stick around to work on the Apple Watch and later the (since abandoned) Apple Car project. Mansfield finally retired in 2020. Cook had a similar experience with Doug Field, who Jobs hired from Segway to head up Mac product design (even though Jobs thought the Segway’s design was bad). Field left Apple for Tesla in 2013, rejoined Apple in 2018, and then went to Ford in 2021 (a role he left last week). Vision Pro leader Dan Riccio, who Bloomberg described as a “key player” under Jobs for his work on hardware engineering, retired in 2024. Last year, Apple lost another old guard executive, former chief operating officer Jeff Williams, who helped bring to life Jobs’ idea of putting a glass screen on the original iPhone. Perhaps the most notable departure in recent years was that of Jony Ive, the legendary Apple designer who called Jobs his “closest” and “most loyal friend.” He left Apple in 2019 after having stepped back for periods of time in the preceding years. That’s not to say there’s no connection to the Jobs era in this new leadership team. Ternus bridges the gap between Jobs and Cook. He joined Apple in 2001 and rose to vice president of hardware engineering under Cook in 2013, overseeing the launch of post-Jobs products like the AirPods and the iPhone Air. Apple’s newly appointed chief hardware officer, Johny Srouji, is in a similar position. He joined Apple to work on the A4 chip in 2008 and went on to launch the company’s first in-house Mac chip in 2020. Sabih Khan, who initially joined Apple in 1995, stepped into the role of chief operating officer last year. Still, as one would expect after 15 years, Apple’s next leadership team is very much the team created by Cook. In many respects, he kept around the Jobs-era crew for a remarkably long time. There remain people on Apple’s leadership team who were there when the company wasn’t the behemoth it is today. But that era of executives is very much winding down. It’s now up to these new leaders to leave their own stamp on Apple. During his tenure, Cook and his team have transformed Apple into a $4 trillion company. With Cook handing Ternus the reins to one of the biggest technology companies in the world, he’ll have some major decisions to make about where to take Apple next.

articles.title: Foldables are sort of boring now — and that’s great news for Apple
articles.summary: The once-novel technology is now refined enough for Apple’s standards.
articles.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on smartphones and Android, follow Dominic Preston. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started Believe it or not, it didn’t all start with Samsung. Royole, a now-bankrupt manufacturer of flexible displays, was the first to release a commercial folding phone, the “charmingly awful” FlexPai. Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold followed a year later, plagued by a variety of faults that saw review units break within days. That launch went so badly that it prompted Chinese rival Huawei to delay the launch of its own Mate X foldable by five months; its unusual design with the foldable screen wrapped around the outside of the phone proved unpopular regardless. Motorola was next to join with its first Razr foldable, closely followed by Samsung’s similar Z Flip; we scored each 4/10 and 6/10 respectively. To say it was a rough first two years for foldable phones would be an understatement, but things did get better. Samsung’s subsequent generations of foldables didn’t break half as easily as the first wave, and it learned the valuable lesson that integral parts of the display stack shouldn’t be as easy to remove as a screen protector. More manufacturers joined the market, with foldables launched by Google, OnePlus, Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi, Honor, and more. Prices slowly came down too — while flagship book-style foldables have hovered more or less around the $2,000 mark for seven years straight, cheaper models have appeared too. Motorola’s entry-level Razr is now $799, and last year Samsung introduced a cheaper FE variant of its Z Flip 7, for $899. The hardware evolved over that period too. Foldables got thinner, lighter, and more durable; the creases got flatter and less visible, while some displays began to include stylus support too; the cameras started to catch up to standard slab phones. Perhaps most importantly, the form factors began to shift too. How it’s going Until recently, foldable phones settled into two broad categories: compact flip phones, by now with square cover screens that extend across the outside of the phone’s front; and larger book-style foldables that are thin when shut and almost square when open. This has slowly begun to change. Huawei was the first to push new designs, starting with its Mate XT trifold, then followed by a wider Pura X flip phone, and this year the Pura X Max, wider still. Samsung launched its own Galaxy Z TriFold late last year, and last month shifted its Galaxy Z Fold 8 to the same squat shape as the Pura X Max. Durability has improved to the point where Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold was able to introduce an IP68 rating; Honor’s Magic V6 has since one-upped that with IP69. That phone is also the thinnest foldable on the market, and the one with the largest battery, two feats that have been made possible by silicon-carbon battery designs, a more energy-dense technology that enables smaller batteries with larger capacities. The latest foldables are barely thicker than flagship slab phones when closed, and almost as thin as the USB-C port when open, while packing batteries that last a day or two per charge. Oppo’s Find N6 is almost as thin and long-lived as the Honor phone, but has another trick up its sleeve: an almost invisible crease. It’s still possible to see and feel the point where the inner screen folds, but only if you really hunt for it, and even then it can often be difficult to find depending on the light. As for cameras, this remains the one area where foldables still have work to do, but not too much. Recent foldables from Oppo and Vivo have had triple rear cameras capable of impressive quality, comparable to some slab flagships. But they still lag behind the top tier of Ultra handsets, while costing substantially more. Still, this may be one area where foldables never fully catch up — cost and design constraints likely mean that the best of the best cameras will be limited to regular phones for the foreseeable future, with foldables always a step or two behind. Despite all these improvements, foldable phones remain an undeniably niche proposition: according to Counterpoint, they made up just 1.6 percent of the smartphone market in 2025. What happens next The tech behind foldable phones is now mature enough for even Apple to trust it: The first foldable iPhone is widely expected to debut next month alongside the iPhone 18 Pro models. The looming launch will be “a turning point for the foldable segment,” according to IDC analyst Francisco Jeronimo, in a report predicting Apple will claim 34 percent of the foldable market by value in its first year. What remains to be seen is whether Apple will have the influence to grow the foldable market, drawing in customers who were skeptical until now, or simply waiting for a foldable that runs iOS. This could be the tipping point that pulls foldables from a niche to the mainstream, though assuming Apple prices the phone at a premium, there will still be pretty strict limits to its reach. Even before its first sale, the foldable iPhone has already had an impact. Remember Huawei and Samsung’s wider folds? It’s probably no surprise that they appeared just months before Apple’s foldable, which leaks suggest will be similarly wide. More companies are likely to jump on the bandwagon, with leaks pointing to wider folds from both Oppo and Honor on the way. The next 12 months will be the test of whether this form factor is truly more popular with users, or if Android manufacturers will regret hopping on the Apple bandwagon. It’s less clear if more manufacturers will be making trifolds, or even whether Huawei and Samsung will stick with that form factor. Huawei has made bullish claims about the sales success of its two Mate XT phones, so there’s hope it will stick with the design. Samsung, on the other hand, pulled its TriFold from the market after less than three months, though it’s unclear if that was down to low sales or simply a small manufacturing run. Rollables and other experimental form factors will likely have to wait a few more years before being commercialized. This is a moment of major change for foldable phones. The standard models have gotten so good that they’ve become a bit boring. Outside of new form factors, the annual releases have settled into a rhythm of minor iteration, and price is now the only real reason for consumers to resist them. Foldables are undeniably good enough now, and Apple’s arrival will either open the market up more widely, or prove once and for all that most phone buyers simply don’t care about phones that fold — or at least not at the prices being charged. By the way * If you’re skeptical that rollable phones are on the way any time soon, remember that it’s been a full year since Lenovo started selling a laptop with a rollable display. * In the early days of foldables the flip form factor was far more popular, but Counterpoint data shows that’s flipped, and it only expects the trend to continue. * When I say the Oppo Find N6’s crease is hard to see, I meant it — I could barely even capture it in photos. It relies on 3D printing a photosensitive liquid polymer that fills every gap in the hinge, then is hardened with a blast of UV light. Read this * There’s a lot we don’t know about Apple’s first foldable, but Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports it will run a version of iOS adapted to deliver an iPad-esque interface, though without the full multitasking features of iPadOS. Oppo’s ColorOS remains the gold standard for foldable software on the Android side, combining flexible split-screen options with floating app windows. * My colleague Allison Johnson became a devotee of working from working from a foldable — or, as she puts it, Purse Computer — and laid out her journey finding a suitable setup * Foldable displays have improved a lot over the last few years, but the basic principles of current designs were set when Samsung introduced a flexible glass screen on the first Galaxy Z Flip. Sean Hollister wrote a great explainer at the time of how exactly Samsung and other manufacturers make glass bend.

articles.title: Distraction-free writing gadget BYOK is adding custom extensions
articles.summary: BYOK’s solution for adding features to its distraction-free writing tool without bloat is an optional scripting system.
articles.body: BYOK is a no-frills, single-purpose gadget that 90 percent of people will find absolutely frivolous. But for those who spend a significant chunk of their lives putting words to virtual paper, there is an obvious allure. Personally, I think it’s at its best when you just stick to the bare minimum, focusing on pure text drafting. Certain users, though, need more. They want BYOK to take notes, they want to use it for writing screenplays, or maybe they want to organize a sprawling novel. Balancing the wants and needs of these more demanding users has been a challenge that BYOK founder Nick Sjolinder has been trying to figure out how to tackle. The answer he seems to have landed on, is scripts. Rather than clutter BYOK with a ton of features that 80 percent of its users wont touch, or crowd the Studio app with even more formats, the company is planning to implement optional scripts that expand the capabilities of BYOK. [Media: A few examples of the kinds of thing people will be able to create are a screenplay assistant, a character note tool, and a writing analyzer. This could let users highlight text in a document and pull it out as a note or tell them when they’re using the passive voice. It’s still early in development and the scripting features haven’t rolled out publicly, but BYOK is asking for feedback from its users.

articles.title: China’s robots race ahead
articles.summary: Bots were breaking records and breaking down at Beijing’s World Humanoid Robot Games.
articles.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on falling robots and the US-China AI race, follow Robert Hart. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started I’ve admitted my fondness for robot fail videos on Stepback before, and let me tell you the World Humanoid Robot Games did not disappoint. [Media: The five-day event, which wrapped this week in Beijing, brought high drama, and brought it well. One robot, made by smartphone maker Honor, lost a leg mid-sprint, while others tripped in a flurry of sparks. Another finisher ran straight into a crash mat, bounced off it, and promptly burst into flames. In the weightlifting, one robot lost its balance beneath a modest barbell and toppled inexorably into the judges’ table, arms cartoonishly aloft. Robotic cheerleaders tumbled and stumbled through routines, while a separate bot fell off a platform in circumstances that, had it been human, might have looked suspiciously like it was gawking at the performers. [Media: This was only the second World Humanoid Robot Games, though it was already far bigger than the inaugural event last year. Unlike this year, last year’s records were paltry. The winning 100-meter sprint was a glacial 21.50 seconds and the highest standing high jump was just 0.95 meters. In keeping with China’s habit of turning robots into public spectacle — from intricate dances at a Spring Festival Gala to demos at major tech events — both this and last year’s games were staged in Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval, a former Olympic venue. And a spectacle it was. At most sporting events, contestants losing limbs, careening into walls, catching fire, and regularly being carried away on stretchers — oh, and did I mention catching fire?! — would probably be grounds to stop proceedings. At the Humanoid Robot Games, it was par for the course. Fire aside, the games were unusual in other ways too. Alongside familiar events like sprinting, football, boxing, and weightlifting were more unusual competitions in bed-making, parcel delivery, shelf stacking, clothes folding, and hammering nails. Aptly, there was a firefighting contest too. These less standard offerings spoke to the real purpose of the games: getting robots out of the lab and into the messy real-world environments their makers hope they will ultimately work in. And China is making no secret of wanting to lead the way. How it’s going For all the spectacle and drama, the games show there has been massive progress in robotics in recent years. Records fell, with one humanoid running the 100-meter sprint in 9.39 seconds, beating Usain Bolt’s 2009 world record. Another bot reached 2.88 meters in a standing high jump, nearly half a meter above the human high-jump record that has stood since 1993. Those performances are almost unrecognizable compared to robotics competitions a decade ago, when even the most advanced machines struggled to stay upright. But the games also show how far there is to go before humanoids are actually useful in the real world. The flashy, video-friendly sporting events were impressive, but the more mundane tasks were less thrilling — I don’t see picking up soybeans with tweezers, block-building, or powder-weighing becoming Olympic mainstays anytime soon. While many events required robots to operate autonomously — including gymnastics, football, tug of war, table tennis, and some track events — others allowed for human assistance via teleoperation, albeit with a scoring penalty. The dexterity being displayed certainly points to genuine and impressive hardware improvements, but seems like there is still a long way to go before these machines can operate reliably on their own in places like factories or homes. What happens next Beijing has not yet confirmed a third Humanoid Robot Games, but given the government’s enthusiasm for the industry, it would be surprising to not get another installment. The city has already confirmed another humanoid half-marathon for April, and the country plans to open its first robot-run hotel next year. China was the undisputed champion of the games, and the country looks well placed to stay in top position moving forward — both at future competitions and in the humanoid robot industry as a whole. The medal table was almost entirely a Chinese affair, dominated in particular by AgiBot and Tien Kung, each scooping up more medals than nearly every other competitor combined, excluding the other. In part, that asymmetry reflected the lack of international competition. Although the games were framed as a global affair, 641 of 666 teams were Chinese, domestically representing 157 companies and 200 universities, according to state-run China Daily. While there doesn’t seem to be a public breakdown of entrants, the biggest US humanoid players like Tesla, Boston Dynamics, and Figure were conspicuous by their absence. Nevertheless, the sheer diversity of Chinese institutions represented in Beijing was a show of force, and a sign of how quickly the country’s robotics sector is maturing, even amid growing concerns about circular investment, thriving companies that lack viable products, and a possible humanoid bubble. It’s not clear a stronger US showing at the games would’ve changed much. The US still has an edge in frontier AI and advanced chips, but China has been rapidly closing parts of that gap, while also making embodied AI a strategic national priority. The same cannot be said of Washington, which has for years paid much less attention to robotics and now trails China in nearly every regard, including manufacturing, deployment, and hardware. Some reports even suggest that recent efforts to ban foreign robots, a general policy squarely aimed at China, could backfire, given how dependent domestic firms are on Chinese components. Catching up to China will take serious and concerted effort, but given how quickly the technology is moving, there’s still time to make up ground. Washington is already treating other areas of AI as strategic priorities in its competition with Beijing; robotics could be one of them. There will be plenty of stumbling along the way, and, hopefully, plenty more robot fail videos too. By the way * DARPA still runs robotics challenges, but they drew far more attention a decade ago. * When the US government banned foreign robots, it didn’t just ban humanoids and quadrupeds. It banned Roombas too, reports The Verge’s own Sean Hollister. * “The brains may come from the US, but the body could very well be Made In China,” writes Business Insider’s Lloyd Lee in a report setting out how the US could do with bolstering its hardware supply chain. * Unlike language models, you can’t simply scrape the internet to build an AI capable of interacting with the real world. A lot of that data has to be generated, which is why companies desperately want to film you doing chores, or send someone to your house to film them doing them. Read this * The Atlantic and the South China Morning Post both have great sets of pictures showing highlights of the games worth checking out. * Why do we keep laughing when robots fail? An old but still good exploration of that shared joy in vintage Vice. * You can learn a lot about a robot by kicking it, says Verge alum James Vincent in an excellent Harper’s feature outlining the state of play in the humanoid industry. * I’m not only about robot fail videos. I can hate them in real life too, as I did with Casio’s fluffy AI pet thing, Moflin.

articles.title: Two new small, powerful Macs
articles.summary: Plus: a new Star Wars game, a Nokia phone that can charge your phone, a Wyze cam with a great privacy feature, and more.
articles.body: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 142, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, how is it almost September already, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.) This week, I’ve been remembering Dolly Parton, Tim Curry, and Peter Cullen, absorbing everything in Rockstar’s big GTA VI preview, wondering if Apple will announce a foldable iPhone at its September event, getting sucked into Summoning Salt’s latest speedrunning documentary about competitive Tetris, listening to Weird Al’s new Tiny Desk concert (“The Saga Begins!”), and getting a Reuben from my favorite local spot after thinking about it for months. This week, I also have for you new Macs, a Nokia phone that can charge your phone, a Wyze cam with a great privacy feature, and more. Programming note: Installer is off next week. I’ll be on vacation. See you next month for Techtember! (As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What do you want to know more about? What are your favorite things you’ve watched / seen / listened to / eaten recently? Drop a line to installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.) The Drop * The M6 and M5 Pro Mac Mini. Apple updated its tiny computer this week, and you can preorder it with a new M6 chip or an M5 Pro. Unfortunately, they have starting prices that are $100 more expensive than the previous generation, and the new model won’t be released until September 22nd. The company also refreshed the Mac Studio, and you can preorder it with a new M5 Ultra chip. * Star Wars: Zero Company. This strategy game set in the Star Wars universe has been getting rave reviews. Gotta find some time to squeeze this in with all of the other big games coming out soon. * HMD’s Nokia 300 Charge. HMD made an old-school, candybar-style Nokia dumbphone that doubles as a power bank. It also has a 3.5mm headphone jack. Who needs a foldable iPhone when you can have this? * Wyze’s Indoor Cam Pan. This new $39.98 security camera can tilt 360 degrees around and 103 degrees vertically, but it also has a privacy mode that tilts the lens fully downward into the body of the camera so that it can’t see anything. Great feature. * Garmin’s Fenix 9 smartwatches. The Fenix 9 and 9 Pro have OLED screens, 64GB of storage, and for the two bigger sizes of the 9 Pro, the option to get solar-charging displays. The watches aren’t cheap, though: The Fenix 9 starts at $999.99, while the Pro starts at $1,099.99. * Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition. The Switch 2 version of FromSoftware’s all-time classic is apparently worth the wait after a big delay. Do I need yet another excuse to get lost in The Lands Between? Probably not, but I’m tempted. * Whoop’s Meridian Band. This $149 band is made from Milanese mesh, comes in gold, rose gold, silver, and black, and makes your fifth-gen Whoop tracker look super fancy. But one part isn’t so fancy: You can’t charge your Whoop while it’s in the Meridian Band. Screen Share Today I’m featuring John Gruber of Daring Fireball. If you follow Apple and are a regular Verge reader (which, as an Installer subscriber, I assume you are), you’re probably well aware of Gruber and his work as a writer, podcaster, friend of the site, and as a general tech person on the internet. Ahead of Apple’s big launch event coming up on September 9th, I thought it would be fun to feature the homescreen of one of the most well-known people in the Apple universe. [Image: The phone: iPhone 17 Pro, deep blue, 1 TB (of which only 200 GB is used, but that won’t stop me from wasting money on a 1 TB model this year too). The wallpaper: My wallpaper is a subtle gradient from very dark gray to black. For years I just stuck with a flat black wallpaper, as god and Steve Jobs intended. (You couldn’t change your homescreen wallpaper until iOS 4, and I remain unconvinced that was a good idea.) I like the subtle gradient now because it lets the dynamic island have a little visual contrast from the wallpaper background. The apps: I’ve currently got three todo/task apps on the homescreen, which I can’t recommend, but it’s currently working for me: Unforgetful, Finalist, and Due. (The red “1” badge on Unforgetful is for a reminder to send you this email and the screenshot of my homescreen.) I’ve also arguably got three notes apps, if you count Journal (in addition to Tot and Apple Notes). Mosaic is a TestFlight-only alternative to the official MLB app, which has a great story behind it. Rather than shutting it down, MLB hired its developer, Jason Weingardt, because Mosaic is so awesome. If I took the screenshot later tonight, you’d see a Live Activity from Mosaic of the Yankees game in the Dynamic Island. Kotoba is also TestFlight-only. It is, in my humble opinion, the best dictionary app for iOS, but because it uses the system-provided dictionaries and thesauruses to act as a dictionary app, it’s not permitted in the App Store. I look up words with it almost every single day. I wrote about it on Daring Fireball a while ago. The Siri app shows that I’m testing the iOS 27 betas. It’s good. I tend to use it side by side with ChatGPT for now, to compare responses, but going forward, I’ll use both. So having that alongside ChatGPT is in line with my having multiple todo apps and multiple note apps (and multiple messaging apps). I keep the badge on Mail counting my unread messages to remind myself that the heat death of the universe is inevitable. Oh, and my App Store app icon isn’t the actual App Store app, but instead a shortcut that jumps me right to the list of apps with pending updates to install. I also asked John to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back: * One show whose second season just finished: The Agency, on Paramount+. I think it’s probably the best spy series ever made. * One show whose sixth season is about to begin: Slow Horses, on Apple TV. I think it’s probably the most amusing spy series ever made. * Third, It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia, whose 18th season just started; it’s the best and most realistic show set in Philadelphia ever made. Crowdsourced Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Bluesky. “Feels like this week is all Dolly Parton, Tim Curry, and now Transformers for Peter Cullen in terms of what people are watching and listening to!” — Carli “I’ve been playing A la Card and REALLY enjoying my time with it. It’s an indie roguelike deck builder game that feels like Slay the Spire and Balatro said ‘Let’s go out for food from a food truck.’ All cards can be mutated and changed via the events — their values, their effect, what triggers them. Great art and music, solid design, and it’s scratching an itch I didn’t know I had. Awesome game from a 2-person indie dev team.” — Tom “My preorder shipped early so I’ve been reading Emo Revival by Andrew Sacher and it’s a 10/10 so far.” — @thoughtlesskyle.bsky.social “Empire of AI, Karen Hao. Recently translated to PT-BR :)” — Milena “Tonight I’m going to finish House of Guinness. It’s a fine show but even better if you drink when watching it.” — Nick “I’ve been on a kick reading older sci-fi novels recently and came across Berserker by Fred Saberhagen (1967). Fantastic book but surprisingly hard to find a physical copy. Ended up purchasing an ePub. Highly recommend!” — Nathan Signing off I got a few good screentime reduction tips following last week’s issue. One person said they don’t install apps with an infinite scroll, which I thought was a good idea. They also have Screen Time enabled to block various things, but their partner holds the password to unlock Screen Time if needed. Clever! Another reader suggested zipping up their phone in a phone pocket. On my vacation next week, to make sure I actually unplug, I plan to deploy my favorite hack: hiding every gadget with a browser in my daughter’s closet. My only free time where I could potentially slip into mindless scrolling would be when she’s sleeping, but there’s no way I’m risking waking her up just to get out the laptop. More time for the important stuff — like playing Switch 2. See you in two weeks!

articles.title: Vivek Dahiya opens up about Divyanka Tripathi’s postpartum recovery after welcoming twins: says ‘It is real’
articles.summary: Popular television couple, Divyanka Tripathi and Vivek Dahiya recently welcomed twin baby boys and are enjoying parenthood. Recently, in an interview,.
articles.body: Popular television couple, Divyanka Tripathi and Vivek Dahiya recently welcomed twin baby boys and are enjoying parenthood. Recently, in an interview, Vivek spoke about how becoming parents has changed their lives. He also talked about postpartum depression and said it is very real.While talking to HindiRush, Vivek spoke about postpartum depression and explained that mothers experience many physical and hormonal changes after childbirth. He added that accepting these changes in their bodies can be one of the biggest challenges they face.He shared, “Postpartum depression is real. Because, you know, there are so many changes. There are hormonal changes. The mother starts realising, ‘My body is no longer the body I had before.’ You know, ‘I now have to live with this.’ And it is very difficult."Vivek further added how after giving birth to twin babies has affected Divyanka's core strength. He also revealed that the actress followed her workout routine regularly but adjusting to the sudden changes in her body was especially difficult for her. He said, "“Suddenly, it feels like jelly here. The core that you had is suddenly not there at all. You can’t even imagine life without your core, especially if you are someone who works out a lot. Your core is involved in everything. So suddenly, your core strength is gone.”The Yeh Hai Mohabbatein actor went on to talk about the uncertainty that comes with postpartum recovery, "On top of that, you have this jelly-like stomach. And you don’t know how you will get back, how you will bounce back, how long it will take. And your daily activity is just around feeding, feeding, feeding, feeding, feeding,” he said.In the interview, Vivek also spoke about the new phase of parenthood, "It’s a completely new phase, and there is a lot for us to learn. As parents, I feel the responsibility has increased because everything is new to us. I make mistakes and learn something new every day while trying to build a bond with my children. They were only three months old recently, so we have already come a long way. They are twins and were premature, so they were extremely tiny when we first held them. Their eyes would not even open properly. In the beginning, it was difficult to fully understand what was happening. But slowly, you realise that this child is now your responsibility for life, and they don’t know anything yet."Vivek described the parenthood phase as learning and beautiful, "For the last one-and-a-half years, I have been attending workshops on AI and learning how to train it by giving it the right prompts. I look at parenting in a similar way. Every day, I think about what I should say or do, what activities I should introduce and what a father should do to help them grow. Hopefully, they will turn out just fine. So, this is a beautiful phase, but it is also a phase of learning something new every day,” he shared.

articles.title: Inside “The Kelly Clarkson Show”’s ‘Bittersweet’ Finale and How Her Kids Supported Her During the Taping (Exclusive)
articles.summary: After seven seasons, the final episode of Kelly Clarkson’s eponymous talk show airs on Monday, Aug. 31
articles.body:
The Kelly Clarkson Show comes to an end on Monday, Aug. 31

PEOPLE attended the finale taping and spoke with the showrunner about the many moments that left an impact throughout the show's seven-season run

"I hope we made things a little bright," says executive producer Alex Duda

After meeting Kelly Clarkson for the first time, the team behind The Kelly Clarkson Show knew their host was special. What they didn't know, however, was that her talents would carry them through seven seasons, secure 24 Daytime Emmy Awards and lead the charge with one of the show's "biggest cultural contributions" in its " Kellyoke " segment.

As Clarkson's eponymous talk show comes to an end on Monday, Aug. 31, showrunner and executive producer Alex Duda feels, all in all, Clarkson was simply superb at her job.

"She was a connector. We learned that very early on," Duda tells PEOPLE. "The way she connected to people — that's why we knew we wanted a format where people sat on the couch next to each other, the celebrity next to the human-interest guest, because when you do that, extraordinary moments can happen that you won't see anywhere else."

Those are the types of moments that were included in Clarkson's farewell-episode taping, which airs on Aug. 31. Back in February, the multi-hyphenate revealed her decision to step back as a daytime host in an effort to prioritize her children. Her final episode is fittingly a celebration of family, as well as the music and the people who kept the show going since it premiered in September 2019.

To mark the occasion, Duda, Clarkson and the team chose to make the final curtain call a "Kelly by Request" show. The special episode, which PEOPLE attended during the taping on June 5, taps a few of Clarkson's biggest fans and some of the folks directly impacted by TKCS 's charitable efforts over the years, to request their favorite songs from her catalog. It was essentially a concert of greatest hits, deep cuts and making-of stories sprinkled in between — featuring one Kellyoke track, "Golden" from KPop Demon Hunters , which Duda teases as the "most requested" ever.

Audience members were reminded throughout the taping that they were indeed the "last audience to see Kelly on this stage."

"We just tried to make it be a celebration, especially that last episode, tried to make that be for the fans and help them help us say goodbye," Duda says. "And for seven years, we listened to them like, 'What songs did you want to hear and what moments did you want to see again?' So it seemed like the right thing to do was to do a whole show that was by request."

Kellyoke, the show's long-running segment in which Clarkson covers other musicians' songs, had a lot to do with that decision, too.

"Music was was basically our shortcut to connection, and I think it was one of our biggest cultural contributions was that our show became that rare place where artists could hear their own music reinterpreted by one of the greatest vocalists of our generation," Duda says. "And then they liked it and they celebrated it. We loved it when artists would tweet, Céline Dion or Coldplay and so many. They loved it."

Among a few of Clarkson's biggest musical moments — including "Since U Been Gone" and "Stronger" – she also wrapped her run with a performance of her new single "I'd Be Lying." During the taping, she ran it back a few times just to make sure it sounded just right as a send-off to the show she's led for seven years.

Clarkson, who called the final taping "bittersweet," had two very special guests in the audience: her two children, River Rose, 12 and Remington Alexander , 10, whom she welcomed with late ex-husband Brandon Blackstock . The final episode featured throwback clips of the kids during their time on the show.

"It's been seven years. We haven't changed a bit, but when you look at River and Remy, you know time has gone by because they're almost grown up and they did so great. They did so great," Duda says of their finale appearance.

Toward the end of her final day on set, Clarkson's children recalled their favorite moments from the series. For River, she told her mom it was, "watching you shine."

While her kids didn't request songs (just some ice cream and a trip to Disney, much to the delight of the audience), Clarkson still ended her daytime run to thunderous applause, on-stage photos with the 200-person crew, and an eventual TKCS staff party filled with what Duda says was "bawling and reminiscing."

"I hope we made things a little bright. Especially in the pandemic, we felt that things were so dark that if we can control this one hour and make the sun shine, then we've accomplished something," the showrunner explains. "And how do you do that? Like I said, music was our touch point all the time."

The secret to the success of TKCS wasn't just the music, or Clarkson's natural ability to make virtually any song her own. It was the celebrities "dropping their guards," and Clarkson's mission to affect change by shining a light on the "heroes" who make up local communities (largely via her memorable Rad Human and Good Neighbors segments).

"She's a mood shifter in the room," Duda says. "And if we could do that for everybody at home, then we've accomplished something."

After more than 1,200 episodes, the finale of The Kelly Clarkson Show airs on Monday, Aug. 31 via NBCUniversal Syndication Studios. Check your local listings.

articles.title: 4 lessons I hope Apple's foldable iPhone takes from the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
articles.summary: If we do get a foldable iPhone soon, I hope it follows Samsung's lead on a few things.
articles.body:
The iPhone launch event is right around the corner on September 9 , and the big rumor is that Apple will reveal its first foldable iPhone this year. If that proves true, Apple will be playing catch up — Samsung, Google, Motorola and others have had foldable phones in their lineups for years. This won't be the first time Apple's coming onto a scene a little late, but I hope it sees this as an opportunity to learn from its peers. Samsung has arguably the strongest foldable lineup right now, and it just added the short-and-stout Galaxy Z Fold 8 this year. That phone impressed me, and I'm hoping Apple can learn a thing or two from Samsung's execution of the Z Fold 8. Here's what I hope Apple takes away from Samsung's newest foldable smartphone.

I loved Flex Mode on previous models of the Galaxy Z Fold and Flip smartphones, but unfortunately, with the Z Fold 8's new hinge design, that feature isn't available. Flex Mode lets you prop up your foldable smartphone in an L-shape so you can use apps both on the top part of the screen and the bottom, or in the case of the camera app, more easily access controls on the bottom part of the screen while using the top part of the screen to frame your shot. It basically gives you two semi-independent displays on a phone that sits upright, allowing you to take better photos and selfies, watch YouTube videos on the top screen while scrolling through comments on the bottom, and more. The built-in stand effect is enough for me to want to use it all the time, and I appreciated how Samsung went out of its way to make sure a lot of its native apps worked with Flex Mode. I would love to see Apple bring this back in its own way.

Lesson 2: App and software compatibility is key.

A big part of any foldable phone is how well its apps and software work across different orientations. Instead of just one, tall, rectangular display, programs will have to work seamlessly across multiple screens of different sizes and aspect ratios. I've been generally impressed with Samsung's execution of this, but of course, they don't control the entire Android ecosystem. Apple, similarly, doesn't control every app in its App Store (as much as it might want to), but I hope that at least most of Apple's native apps will be foldable-ready at launch. A quick way to alienate users to a new smartphone experience is to make their favorite apps more difficult to use on a new device.

Lesson 3: Overall build quality and durability matter.

You might be thinking, "Duh, Apple is known for making great hardware," and you're right. But any first-generation device has the potential to disappoint after it's put through the stress test of actual users. Samsung had seven generations to work out the kinks in its flexible smartphones, and it really shows on its latest devices. Reparability questions aside , the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the best feeling Samsung foldable to date: the hinge feels strong but not stiff, both the interior and exterior screens look great and don't feel fragile, the interior crease is basically nonexistent, and overall, I don't feel like I have to baby that smartphone when I'm using it. Apple has to match that level of build quality out of the gate.

Smartphones are a given in everyday life now, so by nature, any that are difficult to use won't survive. Not only is the Galaxy Z Fold 8 not that, but it's also actually fun to use — it taps into a type of whimsy that tech has lost over the past 5-10 years, so much so that it makes me want to use it more than my main smartphone. Apple has to make its foldable experience easy to adopt and enjoyable enough that users get some of that early-days wonder back. That means nailing the basics — performance, design, battery life and app compatibility — and putting its own flair on things that will make people stop and think "maybe I do want my next phone to be foldable."

articles.title: Read Tim Cook’s final message to Apple staff as CEO
articles.summary: “I love this company and the team behind it.”
articles.body: Steve Jobs’ successor carried the torch of the iPhone and built Apple into a global powerhouse with few rivals. Since becoming CEO in 2011, Tim Cook has led the company to become one of the most dominant forces in the daily lives of billions of people. Today is his last day as CEO. [Media: We’ll have a lot to say about new Apple CEO John Ternus as the change happens. For now, you can read Cook’s final letter to Apple staff below, as reported by Bloomberg and 9to5Mac: > Team, > Today is my last day as CEO of Apple. This is a moment I always knew would come one day, and yet it is still hard to believe it has arrived and I am writing these words. I love this company and the team behind it, and I couldn’t let this day pass without sending a note to you, to tell you how grateful I am for the outpouring of affection you’ve sent my way, for the way you’ve shown up each and every day, and most of all, for the privilege of a lifetime serving as your leader. > The truth is, whatever there is to say about my success, I know it is all because of you. You have brought out the best in me. In all my life, I have never seen or been with such an extraordinary team of people before, and every day I get to see more examples of that. > There is something truly special about Apple. I am most proud of what an annual report could never capture. This place is proof that culture triumphs over everything. We share a belief that what we build matters, and that we have both the opportunity and the responsibility to leave the world better than we found it. That purpose is part of what makes this place extraordinary. Apple helps nurture it, but I believe it lived within each of you long before you arrived here. It is what brought you to this company and what continues to drive the work you do every day. Together, we have created something far greater than any one of us could have imagined or accomplished alone. And that’s the secret to our success. We bring out the best in each other. articles.title: Tim Cook's parting message: Apple is in the hands of a product builder | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Tim Cook’s farewell memo to Apple employees offers a glimpse at how he wants John Ternus to be seen: as a product builder with deep experience across the iPhone, Mac, AirPods, and other major hardware lines.
articles.body:
On his last day as Apple CEO, Tim Cook offered a rousing endorsement of his successor: John Ternus , the company’s senior vice president of hardware engineering. In a memo to employees, Cook reminded staff that he’s “not leaving Apple,” just stepping away from the role of CEO, while declaring that “few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does.”

Ternus’ elevation to the top job suggests that Apple’s next era will see a renewed focus on hardware and product execution. Under Ternus, Apple shipped a number of notable products, most recently, the new ultra-thin iPhone Air, the lower-cost MacBook Neo, and AirPods with hearing health features. He also led the hardware engineering team across Apple’s full device lineup.

Hardware will play an important role in the AI era, not only in terms of chips, but also the devices people use to run enterprise AI. Apple this year, for instance, offered earlier releases of its new Mac models, the Mac mini and Mac Studio, compared with years past, driven by AI demand.

Cook’s memo, reported by Bloomberg and others, naturally says little about Apple’s future when it comes to AI, services, regulation, China, or the other challenges that lie ahead. Instead, Cook focuses on his gratitude for the opportunity to lead Apple and exalts the company’s culture as ultimately what matters most.

“We share a belief that what we build matters and that we have both the opportunity and the responsibility to leave the world better than we found it,” Cook wrote. He also referenced the famous Steve Jobs quote about leaving a “dent in the universe,” saying that Apple makes that possible because of “who we are and what we believe,” as well as “what we value and how we see the world.”

Cook will remain at Apple as executive chairman and will continue to manage political relationships, including those with President Trump and the Chinese government.

On X, Cook also wrote : “Sending lots of love to the Apple community on my last day as CEO. My title changes tomorrow, but the love I have for the Apple community never will. Thank you for being a constant source of inspiration. My gratitude is endless, and I’m excited for the next chapter!”

articles.title: Car owners want tech they can ignore
articles.summary: Car owners don’t mind more tech in their vehicles, as long as its easy to ignore, according to a new survey from JD Power.
articles.body: Automakers keep shoving more tech into their cars, despite evidence that consumers are increasingly fed up with huge screens and glitchy software. In fact, the features that car owners appreciate the most happen to be the ones they barely notice, according to the latest tech survey from JD Power. The consumer research firm surveyed 68,084 owners of new 2026 model-year vehicles after 90 days of ownership. The survey touched on 40 automotive technologies covering comfort and convenience; connected vehicles; driver assist; electric vehicles; and smart vehicles. The features that scored the highest were the ones that were the most inconspicuous, like smart ignition, in which the vehicle automatically starts and turns off based on driver actions, or smart HVAC systems, which use AI to automatically adjust the cabin environment for maximum comfort and efficiency. These were the big winners in JD’s survey — mostly because they require the least attention from the driver. Smart ignition, in particular, delivered the highest overall satisfaction, with only 2.4 problems per 100 vehicles. “For automakers, the opportunity is to prioritize technology that makes driving simpler, not more complicated,” Doron Hikry, director of customer success at JD Power, said in a press release. “The features that solve real problems without adding effort or stress for the driver are the ones resonating most with customers.” Superfluous tech features like passenger screens, in which an extra screen is embedded in the dash in front of passengers, rated the lowest in satisfaction. These screens first began cropping up in premium brands, like Mercedes, BMW, and Porsche, but have yet to bleed over to more mass-market vehicles. Apparently, they’re just wasted space on the dash, with more than one-third of owners who have a passenger screen reporting they’ve never tried to use it. Only 6 percent admitted to using their passenger screens every time they drive. Yikes. Another tech feature that has more work to do in winning over customers is hands-free driving, also known as Level 2 Plus automation. These are features like Tesla’s Full Self-Driving, Ford’s BlueCruise, GM’s Super Cruise, and Mercedes’ Drive Pilot. Unlike Level 2 systems, which require drivers to keep their hands on the steering wheel, these L2 Plus systems allow for completely hands-free driving on certain roads. Car owners told JD Power they preferred L2 systems in terms of design and quality of experience, suggesting that more automation does not necessarily mean more customer satisfaction. Interestingly, Level 2 systems were recording slightly higher problems per 100 vehicles (14.3) as L2 Plus ones (13.8). “The results indicate that owners may currently be more comfortable with systems that clearly assist the driver rather than those that introduce a greater degree of automation,” said Hikry. What these results suggest is that car owners don’t necessarily mind more technology in their vehicles, just as long as they don’t make the task of driving more complicated. The individual awards underscore this point: The Cadillac Escalade and Toyota Tundra both won for camera mirrors, while other automakers notched wins for blind-spot cameras, digital keys, one-pedal driving, and EV charging schedulers.

articles.title: Rohit Sharma makes TV debut with 'Family Full House'; Revives his viral ‘Garden’ dialogue
articles.summary: Former Indian cricket skipper Rohit Sharma is making his television debut in the entertainment sector with a new show, 'Family Full House with Rohit S.
articles.body: Former Indian cricket skipper Rohit Sharma is making his television debut in the entertainment sector with a new show, 'Family Full House with Rohit Sharma'. The makers have been teasing fans with interesting promos for the last few months and finally the wait is over. The makers announced the show's title on Monday, along with the premiere date. 'Family Full House' is slated to premiere on 19th September 2026.In the announcement promo, Rohit Sharma is seen meeting fans who request the Indian captain to repeat his famous "garden" and "gully cricket" lines. Rohit, visibly troubled, says, "Do line kya bol di, itna viral ho gaya. Jab mera pura show aayega to kya hoga (I spoke just two lines and it went so viral. What will happen when my entire show comes out)?"In an earlier promo released in May, the makers had used Rohit's viral "garden" dialogue. In the video, he was seen shouting, "Koi bhi garden mein nahi ghumega (Nobody will stroll in the garden)."Cricket lovers are eagerly waiting to see whether the 39-year-old player will be part of the 2027 World Cup. During his recent tour to England, it was speculated that the series decider would be Rohit's last international match for the country. However, Rohit ended up scoring 138 in the 388 chase against England, finishing the England ODIs with 175 runs in three matches at an average of 58.33 and a strike rate of 98.31.The channel airing Rohit Sharma's show already has an interesting lineup. It further includes the latest season of the reality game show 'Kaun Banega Crorepati', hosted by Bollywood legend Amitabh Bachchan, and the 'Indian Game Show' hosted by popular television couple Bharti Singh and Harsh Limbachiyaa. The show has some popular faces from the television world coming together for fun challenges.Rohit has already announced his retirement from Test and T20 cricket formats. However, he continues to be an ODI player.

articles.title: JMGO’s very bright all-in-one projector looks ideal for gamers and sports
articles.summary: The Iris Ultra Max brings 4K, 120Hz, VRR, ALLM, 6500 ISO lumens, and dual-iris contrast control.
articles.body: JMGO’s 4K 120Hz Iris Ultra Max all-in-one Google TV projector is now available outside China. It gets its name from a new dual-iris system that lets it produce an impressive 10,000:1 native contrast, according to JMGO. It boosts the contrast — always an issue with projectors — by placing two separate physical apertures (irises) along different points of the internal optical path to control light scatter and brightness far more aggressively than a single iris can. It also promises to produce a very bright 6,500 ISO lumen image from its triple-laser light engine. Last year at IFA, 6,000 lumens from an all-in-one projector was breaking new ground. At IFA 2026, it’s shaping up to be table stakes, alongside 4k imagery purring along at a smooth 120Hz for fast-moving sports and gaming. Just note that I found JMGO’s N3 Ultimate to be unwatchable at peak brightness due to color distortion — so best wait for the reviews on this one. Like that previous flagship, the new Iris Ultra Max is mounted on a motorized pan-and-tilt gimbal for useful Wiimote-like control. That, combined with an 0.88–1.7:1 optical zoom and V±130% / H±53% lens shift, gives you unparalleled image placement options that also preserve optical image quality. [Image: A look around back. JGMO’s also tossing in VRR and ALLM to keep latency low and reduce tearing when gaming on the IRIS Ultra Max, with support for Dolby Vision HDR at 4K 120Hz. It will eventually list for $3,499, but that drops to $2,999 for preorders that begin today, ahead of an October 19th ship date.
